newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Envoy seeks Albania aid, Socialists control police.
newsitem.headline: Envoy seeks Albania aid, Socialists control police.

text.p: European envoy Franz Vranitzky called for economic aid to underpin Albania's largely peaceful general election and Socialist leader Fatos Nano said his party, headed for victory, had taken control of the police.
President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, its leaders resigned to going into opposition, said it would challenge results in some areas where violence was deemed to have hindered campaigning.
Vranitzky, who brokered a deal between Albania's squabbling political parties in March to hold the early election, met briefly with Berisha and interim Prime Minister Bashkim Fino.
The former Austrian chancellor said Berisha told him that he accepted the Democrats' defeat in Sunday's vote.

But Vranitzky, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe mission with 450 observers, said Berisha gave no indication whether he would step down after five years in power. "No, he did not mention it and I did not ask him," he said.
Diplomatic sources said the president looked tired and glum during the meeting with Vranitzky.

Berisha admitted on television on Monday that the Democrats had lost and many Albanians interpreted the statement as a hint that he was stepping down. As head of state, he has to wait for parliament to convene before he can offer his resignation.
Results declared in 25 of 115 districts run under majority rules confirmed a big swing to the Socialists. They won 13 seats, with two more going to their Social Democratic allies.
The Democrats captured three seats and the remaining seven go to a run-off next Sunday because no candidate won the 50 percent required for victory in the first round.

In proportional voting for 40 seats, partial results gave the Socialists and two allied parties 53 percent of the vote, compared to 30 percent for the Democrats. The Socialists stood to improve their score as results came in from southern regions hostile to the president.
Vranitzky said the election was "a first step...towards reconstructing Albania," to be followed up by Western-backed moves to rebuild the economy and reform institutions.
"It has to be made quite clear that once the elections are over...that everyone in the international community is not going to pack their suitcases and go home," Vranitzky said.
Nano told reporters that Interior Minister Belul Celo had left Albania and Fino had replaced him with his second-in-command, a Socialist Party member.
The new acting minister, Lush Perpali, immediately met officials of the presidential guard and told them to perform their duties regardless of who was minister.
"He said a democratic alternative was the most natural thing in the world and asked them to stay calm," Nano said.
The Interior Ministry refused comment on the appointment. But within minutes of Nano's announcement, police armoured vehicles roared down Tirana's boulevards in a show of force.

Nano said shooting in the capital stopped on Monday evening when Tirana's new police chief, appointed on Monday, sent armoured vehicles to central Skanderbeg Square. Police said a 16-year-old boy was killed by a stray bullet.

The Democrats' secretary general, Genc Pollo, said his party wanted a rerun of voting in more than 20 districts in southern Albania, the centre of months of armed upheaval in which more than 1,500 people were killed earlier this year.

"We cannot accept the result in those areas," he told a news conference. "The courts will have to decide." Pollo also said the vote, described by the OSCE as "adequate and acceptable", was no fairer than last year's election.
The 1996 vote was won by the Democrats but boycotted by the Socialists and dismissed as flawed by international observers.
